#480. Is Spotify still tracking your listening for Wrapped 2026? Heres what we know.

Every year, as Spotify Wrapped season approaches, a familiar kind of panic sets in. You start mentally calculating how many times you've streamed your favorite artist, wondering whether that one song you played obsessively in Feb. will come back to haunt you, and perhaps making a last-minute attempt to influence your results.

Recently, someone asked me who I thought my top artist would be this year, and for the first time in a long time, I genuinely had no idea. Stray Kids have held that spot for the past four years, but with fewer new releases from the group in 2026, my listening habits have been a little more unpredictable. I've spent the year bouncing between artists and genres, which means my top five could be anyone's guess. (And yes, I'm a little nervous about that.)

After all, Spotify Wrapped isn't just a recap of what you listened to. It's become a public declaration of your musical identity, one that inevitably ends up on Instagram Stories for everyone to judge.

But with Nov. nearly over and Spotify Wrapped 2026 expected to arrive in early Dec., there's one important question: Is Spotify still tracking your listening habits?

Spotify has not confirmed the exact cutoff date for Wrapped 2026. However, based on how the company has handled previous editions, your listening data likely stopped counting sometime in mid-Nov.

For years, a persistent rumor suggested that Spotify stopped collecting data for Wrapped on Oct. 31, leaving the final two months of the year out of your annual recap. But that's not quite how it works.

In 2025, Spotify confirmed that Wrapped included listening activity from Jan. 1 through mid-Nov., just a few weeks before its Dec. 3 release. The company explained that it needs time to process listening data and prepare millions of personalized recaps ahead of launch.

So while Spotify continues recording your listening activity for its regular features and recommendations, that doesn't necessarily mean your late-Nov. streams will count toward Wrapped 2026.

Until Spotify confirms this year's tracking window, there's no way to know for certain.

If you're hoping to push a particular artist into your top five before Wrapped arrives, you may already be out of luck.

Even if Spotify is still counting streams, a few days of obsessive listening probably won't dramatically change the habits you've accumulated over the past 11 months.

But there's an important distinction between how Spotify calculates your top songs and top artists. According to Spotify's explanation of its Wrapped methodology, your top songs are ranked by the number of times you've listened to them, with each play counting after more than 30 seconds. Your top artists, meanwhile, are determined using a weighted stream count that gives primary artists more credit than featured performers.

That means an artist whose entire discography you've been listening to all year could rank higher than someone responsible for your single most-played song.

In other words, your Wrapped results aren't necessarily as straightforward as counting how many times you've played your favorite track.

Maybe you're less concerned about getting your favorite artist to No. 1 and more worried about the songs you don't want showing up in your results. Fortunately, Spotify gives users some control over what influences their Wrapped.

In a Nov. 5 announcement, Spotify reminded listeners that they can exclude individual tracks and playlists from their Taste Profile, preventing those streams from influencing certain Wrapped results and everyday recommendations.

Open Spotify and find the track or playlist.

Select "Exclude from your taste profile." (You can reverse the decision by selecting "Include in your taste profile.")

Spotify says this setting applies to past and future listening, meaning you can remove a particularly embarrassing musical obsession from your taste-based results even after you've spent hours streaming it.

There's also a dedicated setting for kids' and family music, which is especially useful for parents who don't want their children's favorite songs dominating their year-end recap.

One caveat: Excluded listening can still contribute to your total minutes listened. It just won't shape your taste-based rankings.

Spotify hasn't announced an official release date, but Wrapped typically arrives in late Nov. or early Dec.

Last year's edition launched on Dec. 3, while the 2024 and 2023 editions arrived on Dec. 4 and Nov. 29, respectively. If Spotify follows its recent pattern of Wednesday releases, Dec. 2, 2026, is a possibility, though the company has yet to confirm that date.

Until then, you can keep listening to whatever you want. Whether those streams make it into your Wrapped is another question entirely.

And perhaps that's for the best. The fun of Spotify Wrapped has always been discovering what your listening habits reveal about you, even when the results aren't quite what you expected.

#476. Lowe's posts strong online sales, raises outlook despite slow housing market

Lowe's on Wednesday posted strong quarterly results and raised its full-year outlook as the company said it saw strength among professional shoppers.

The company said comparable sales grew 1.8% for the fiscal third quarter, driven by a 17.4% increase in online sales and "solid" performance in pro and home services sales. Net sales rose to $22.76 billion.

Because of the strength, Lowe's now said it expects full-year sales of roughly $92.5 billion, up from a previous projection of $92 billion. It also expects comparable sales to be up 0.5%, compared with previous guidance of flat.

CEO Marvin Ellison told CNBC that the company is focused on growing despite economic headwinds and a sluggish housing market. He said Lowe's posted its sixth straight quarterly comparable sales increase and saw particular strength in appliances, which saw its largest revenue growth in five years.

"We believe irrespective of the macro environment we're in, we're going to take share because there's a lot of share out there that we can go and get, and we're going to be aggressive to go and get that share," Ellison told CNBC.

Lowe's also reported a pretax benefit of approximately $250 million from tariff refunds during the quarter, which contributed a 34-cent boost to earnings per share. Ellison said the company plans to use those funds to enhance the customer experience and bring value to shoppers.

He added that do-it-yourself customers and pro shoppers are not investing in major renovation projects but are instead spending on repair and maintenance projects.

"We are giving those pros what they need," he said. "We're able to improve our fulfillment capabilities and our pro loyalty program."

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

For the quarter ended Oct. 30, Lowe's reported net income of $1.67 billion, or $2.98 per share, compared with $1.62 billion, or $2.88 per share, the year prior.

The home improvement retailer has previously said it's seeing "pressure" on spending on projects, especially as consumers are stretched thin by inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty. The company is also battling a slower housing market and higher mortgage rates.

Ellison previously told CNBC he expects consumers to remain cautious through the end of the year.

Lowe's executives said on a call with analysts Wednesday that the company is continuing to battle high fuel costs, which they said accelerated through the third quarter. CFO Brandon Sink said diesel prices are currently around $6 per gallon, up about 15% overall compared to what the company saw in the second quarter.

"So we're trying to continue to manage that, balance that, and we're reflecting that into our Q4 guide," Sink said.

Ellison told CNBC the company remains optimistic about consumer spending this holiday season and that November sales are in line with expectations so far.

Lowe's competitor Home Depot said earlier this week that it's seeing resilience among professional shoppers and reported comparable sales growth.

#474. Target shares rise 7% as retailer posts best sales growth in five years, hikes guidance

Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnaround strategy taking hold.

The retailer said its net sales grew 7.1% during the fiscal third quarter. Comparable sales rose 5.6%, compared with StreetAccount estimates of up 3.8%. That growth was boosted by a 5% increase in comparable traffic, Target added.

"[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters.

Digital comparable sales jumped nearly 10% during the quarter.

Encouraged by the growth, Target raised its full-year guidance, upping its net sales growth guidance by 1 percentage point to around 6%. It's also expecting full-year operating income margin rate to be around 6.2%, which includes roughly 1.1 percentage points of benefit from tariff refunds.

The company also said it's now projecting full-year earnings per share to be in a range of $10.65 to $11.40, compared with prior guidance of between $9.90 and $10.90.

"The changes we've made across our assortment and guest experience are adding up," Fiddelke told reporters. "While we're encouraged by the progress, we know there's more work ahead to sustain this momentum and deliver consistent growth over time."

Target shares climbed about 7% in afternoon trading Wednesday.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

For the quarter ended Oct. 31, Target reported net income of $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, up from $689 million, or $1.51 per share, a year earlier.

This year, the company said it's invested approximately $3.8 billion in capital expenditures, up nearly $1 billion from last year. Because of those returns, Fiddelke said Target is now expecting to invest between $5 billion and $6 billion in capex next year.

On a call with analysts, he added that those investments will go toward more store remodels, technology, supply chain improvements, among other initiatives.

The company said it saw particular strength in beauty, which saw 9% growth, and food and beverage, where sales increased nearly 7%. The retailer added that net sales rose in all three months of the third quarter, with the strongest performance during the back-to-school season.

Fiddelke told reporters the quarter's strength showed "continued progress" toward Target's priorities that it outlined at the beginning of its turnaround.

As it looks to the holiday season, Target said it's marketing thousands of products priced at $5 and under, along with new artificial intelligence-powered shopping experiences to drive engagement. Fiddelke said Target is "encouraged" by shopping behaviors it's seen so far in the current quarter.

The big-box retailer has been showing signs of returning to growth, as it sees stronger sales trends after years of flat revenue. The results come after Target last quarter hiked its full fiscal-year outlook and said it saw "broad-based" strength across its various categories.

It's also lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in an effort to get customers back into its stores, especially as consumer sentiment lags and inflation remains high. The retailer said on Wednesday that it cut prices on an additional roughly 2,000 items during the third quarter.

Target's stock is up more than 70% this year.

#473. Russian ornithologist jailed over small donations to Navalny's foundation

Sofia Rosenfeld has devoted her life to studying Arctic birds. A Russian court sentenced her to 3.5 years in a penal colony over donations to Navalny's foundation. Friends and family are fighting for her release.

Boris Rosenfeld shows DW a photo of him with his daughter Sofia and can't hold back tears. "This was the last time we saw her. Then she left for Moscow, and this whole case began," he says.

Helives in Israel, while Sofia is in Russia. For more than a month now, she has been behind bars on charges of financing extremism. The case goes back to two donations totaling 2,000 rubles (about $30) to the late opposition politician Alexei Navalny'sAnti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which the Russian authorities have since designated as extremist.

On October 7, a court in Moscow sentenced Rosenfeld to three and a half years in a penal colony.

Rosenfeld is a prominent ornithologist who has devoted her life to studying and protecting Arcticbirds. "Sofia was an avid young naturalist from childhood. She loved birds, horses and dogs," her father said as he leafed through a photo album.

Sofia was a teenager when the family moved to Israel but she returned to Russia a few years later and now holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship.

She studied biology at Moscow State University and developed a significant scientific career in Russia. Her colleague, Alexandra Panyutina, who now also lives in Israel, explained that Rosenfeld was devoted to her work from an early age.

"Birds and the Arctic are the defining passions of her life," she said.

Rosenfeld was among the first Russian researchers to develop a systematic approach to monitoring migratory bird populations. To support her research, she even developed a special aircraft.

"They could fly at almost the same speed as the birds and observe them from a low altitude," says Dmitry (name changed), a colleague of Rosenfeld's. "It quickly became clear that this was a unique method."

Rosenfeld is considered to be one of the leading figures in Russian ornithology. Her work has extended well beyond Russia and she has been deeply involved in international research projects. In the field of migratory bird conservation, cross-border cooperation is essential.

Helmut Kruckenberg, the head of the German Institute for Wetlands and Waterbird Research (IWWR), said Rosenfeld was highly respected within the international scientific community.

"She has done an enormous amount for nature conservation and for the protection of Siberian and Arctic species," he said. "What is happening to her is simply beyond comprehension for us."

In the summer of 2021, when Russian authorities designated Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, also known as FBK, as an extremist organization, Rosenfeld was on a remote Arctic expedition without a phone or access to the internet. Therefore, she did not cancel her regular donations to the FBK immediately, doing so only after her return to the Russian capital Moscow.

Her friend Olga (name changed) described Sofia as a person of absolute honesty. According to her, Rosenfeld's donations to Navalny's foundation reflected a genuine desire to fight corruption. Through her work in Russia's regions, she had seen plenty of it firsthand.

"She was never involved in political activism. Her donations were solely intended to support anti-corruption work," said her father Boris Rosenfeld. "It's unthinkable".

For him and others close to her, the sentence came as a shock. Although prosecutors had requested a five-year prison term, friends and colleagues expected that she would receive a fine at most.

There were reasons for that expectation. According to calculations by independent media outlet Mediazona, about 85% of convictions in the 225 cases involving donations to Navalny's foundation have so far resulted in non-custodial sentences. Yet Rosenfeld got three and a half years in a penal colony.

Just a few months after Rosenfeld defended her doctoral dissertation in October 2025, her home was searched. She was also subject to travel restrictions. She continued to work but she had to cancel her annual summer expedition to the Arctic.

Even on the day of the sentencing, her conversations with  her colleagues focused largely on science:  "We discussed how the work could continue in Sofia's absence," Olga said. "But no one really believed she would end up in prison."

"The only thing we think about now is how to bring her here," Boris Rosenfeld says as he looks at the pictures from Sofia's last visit.

Friends and colleagues who spoke to DW say that his daughter never considered leaving Russia, even as the prospect of a prison sentence loomed. "Sofia would never have left. She simply can't imagine life without geese," says Dmitry.

Now, her family, friends and colleagues are campaigning to have her sentence overturned. More than 1,000 people have signed an appeal to Russia's Presidential Council for Human Rights.

Boris Rosenfeld is also hoping for support from Israel but so far Israeli consular officials have not been granted access to his daughter in detention.

The two continue to write to each other and he is trying to keep his spirits high: "She writes that she's trying to adjust to life in prison, and that it's hard," he says. "But she's a strong person."

#467. Jensen Huang is set to testify before the Senate, and he has some explaining to do

If you thought the Jensen Huang saga was over when he stepped down as Nvidia's CEO, think again. Less than two weeks later, Nvidia gave him his job back.

And within hours of Monday's surprise announcement, senators set a date to question him in public — and under oath.

Huang, who co-founded chipmaker Nvidia, is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Thursday, Dec. 3, at 10 a.m. ET, just two days after he's scheduled to speak with various committees of the U.S. House of Representatives. He’s the only witness listed for the hearing, which will focus on U.S. rules limiting where companies can sell their most advanced AI chips. If you want to watch, the committee will be livestreaming the hearing on its website.

Huang has already returned to the Nvidia office, where he was welcomed by cheering employees.

"I'm going to be a better CEO the second time around," he told workers, as seen in a video on X.

Meanwhile, President Trump is taking personal credit for negotiating Huang's return to Nvidia. In a Truth Social post, the president said he assured the Nvidia board that Huang did not pose a national security risk.

President Trump also posted a picture of Jensen Huang photoshopped into his assassination attempt scene while holding up a red bra with an Nvidia flag in the background. Yes, really.

The questions about Nvidia's chips go back well before Huang initially stepped down. In 2024, federal investigators began looking into whether Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer based in Singapore, had sent advanced AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export rules. That investigation took on new significance when reports surfaced that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, who used to run Megaspeed. Jensen Huang acknowledged the affair, and U.S. authorities suspect Alice Huang of working for Chinese intelligence, according to the New York Times (though China has since denied that she was a spy).

The newly empowered House Democrats also have questions for Huang, including whether Nvidia interfered with that investigation. In a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, they asked whether his department had allowed Nvidia to intervene in the Megaspeed probe. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Lawmakers are also looking into exactly how Huang got his job back and what role the Trump administration played.

Just days before Nvidia brought him back, the board had made clear it had no plans to reinstate him, despite Huang saying he would be "honored" to return. On the company's earnings call on Nov. 17, board chair Harvey Jones even said, "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Yet, on Nov. 23, the board voted unanimously to do just that. In a statement, the board wrote that it had heard from senior U.S. officials, and "based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Harvey Jones said in the statement.

Trump had already signaled he was open to Huang getting his job back. On Nov. 16, he told reporters he "would not mind" if Huang returned as CEO and said Huang had "learned a big lesson."

By Monday, Trump was taking credit for the decision. He told CNBC he'd pushed Nvidia's board to bring Huang back. Asked whether the board would have done so without him, Trump said, "The answer is no. I believe my intervention was very important." He also posted on Truth Social, writing, "The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO… Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World!"

That leaves lawmakers in both parties asking what changed. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) called the decision "reckless" and asked the administration to name the officials who spoke to Nvidia and explain what they told the board. Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) asked, "No national security risk? Based on what?" he wrote on X.

Huang had already agreed to answer questions from House lawmakers before he got his job back. That interview is still set for Tuesday, Dec. 1, two days before the public Senate hearing. He’ll meet with three House committees behind closed doors, and the interview will be transcribed.

But now, Huang could also be answering a new set of questions in public about the affair that helped cost him his job and the president who says he got it back for him. So far, Nvidia and Trump have told their sides of the story. The hearing is a chance to hear Huang's.

#466. Nvidia Is Powering Brain-Computer Interfaces Now

A Michigan woman named Mary has a chip in her brain roughly the size of a dime. Though she struggles to speak due to motor neuron disease, the implant allows her to express her thoughts through a synthesized voice on a computer.

Made by brain-computer interface company Paradromics, the implant is outwardly invisible, but the speech decoding requires a cart full of electronics. A year from now, however, that cart will be transformed into a small box that can sit on her wheelchair, thanks to technology from Nvidia. Eventually, those electronics will be so small they’ll fit in a phone, says Paradromics CEO and founder Matt Angle.

Today, Austin-based Paradromics announced a partnership with the AI chipmaker to use Nvidia’s hardware and software to process its brain data. Nvidia is facing a major leadership shakeup and federal scrutiny following longtime CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Though Mary has lost much of the use of her speaking muscles, neurons in her brain still fire when she attempts to speak. The Paradromics implant uses more than 400 embedded electrodes to capture those signals, and a computer uses artificial intelligence to make inferences about what she’s trying to say. The words appear on a screen, and the computer speaks the words for her.

That decoding process takes an incredible amount of computing power. The cart of electronics has to be plugged into an electrical outlet, and Mary must be within range of the cart in order to use her brain-computer interface.

“We're producing a huge amount of data that has a lot of value, but we need to translate that neural data into applications in order to make this a really effective platform,” Angle says. It’s why he calls brain-computer interfaces the ultimate case for edge computing, a distributed computing model that processes and stores data in physical devices close to where it is generated rather than sending it to a distant cloud or data center.

“We want to be able to do it through increasingly smaller and lower-power devices, and the people leading in that area are Nvidia,” he says.

Making brain-computer interfaces practical and portable for patients is a major challenge for the field. While these setups have become far more streamlined since their early days in academic labs, they still require lots of external electronics. Shrinking them down and reducing their power requirements would allow patients to be more mobile with these devices, using them wherever they go.

Paradromics plans to do that by using Nvidia’s Jetson, a low-powered computing module that will allow speech decoding to be done in a small device close to the user. It will also use Holoscan, Nvidia’s AI sensor processing software, to allow users to interact with computers and other devices with low lag time. Brain-computer interfaces will need to work alongside other sensors, such as cameras and microphones, and Holoscan will help process these different data streams together so applications can respond to both neural signals and the context around them.

“Brain-computer interfaces must translate complex neural signals into meaningful actions in real time. Even small delays can make communication feel unnatural,” David Niewolny, Nvidia’s director of business development for health care and medical, tells WIRED via email. “Neural signals also change over time, requiring AI that can continuously adapt to the individual.” Nvidia’s technology processes neural signals and runs AI models in real time.

Reducing lag time is important for a brain-computer interface with a speech function so that users can have naturally flowing conversation without delays.

Through the partnership, Paradromics will also be able to integrate Nvidia’s foundation models into its brain-computer interface. Vikash Gilja, chief scientific officer at Paradromics, says AI models could help make synthesized voices more expressive and human-like. Also, if these models are running locally on Nvidia hardware, it means users won’t have to be connected to the internet in order to use their devices.

Niewolny says he sees “tremendous potential for AI to expand human capability.” Nvidia is working with other players in the brain-computer interface space, including Synchron. The chipmaker will not have access to brain data through these partnerships, he says.

#463. Germany's religious freedom report: Authoritarian regimes, holy wars, and spies abroad

Harassment, persecution, surveillance: Across much of the world, people of faith are facing growing pressure. A new German government report is unusually direct in criticizing China in particular.

The report spans more than 150 pages, but its conclusion can be summed up in a single sentence: "The global situation regarding freedom of religion and belief deteriorated during the reporting period," said Thomas Rachel, the German government's commissioner for freedom of religion and belief, and a member of parliament for the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Recently adopted by the Cabinet, the government's fourth report on the subject covers developments from 2023 to 2025.

The government has issued a dedicated report on freedom of religion and belief around the world. According to the report, this freedom is facing "increasing pressure" globally. The focus is not primarily on the suppression of religious institutions or structures, but on the situation of individuals who hold a religious belief, or none at all.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The importance of religious freedom is reflected in the way the government commissioner describes the issue: "Religion and faith are of great importance to four out of five people around the world and are central to their identity. People wake up with God and go to sleep with God. It is part of their everyday lives." Research by the Pew Research Center suggests that about 84% of the world's population identifies with a certain religion.

At a time when authoritarian regimes are gaining ground and expanding their surveillance capabilities, the report paints a bleak picture. The growing number of violent conflicts, the rise of authoritarian rule, and the spread of populism have led to "painful restrictions on freedom of religion and belief around the world."

The German government report does not attempt to provide a statistical tally of attacks or the number of people facing persecution. Instead, it examines 30 countries as case studies where, in the federal government's view, freedom of religion and belief is being restricted. These include about six countries each from Africa, Asia, and the Arab world. In Europe, the report focuses on Belarus, Russia, Ukraine, and Turkey, while in Latin America it highlights Mexico, Nicaragua, and Cuba. It also identifies shortcomings in five of the world's six most populous countries: China, India, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Nigeria.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Regarding India, the report refers to "Hindu nationalist efforts" that threaten the equal treatment of all officially recognized religions. It states that the generally peaceful coexistence of different faiths is "repeatedly overshadowed by tensions and, at times, violence." Both Muslim and Christian communities report growing intolerance and hate speech. According to the report, violent Hindu extremist groups have carried out a "large number of physical attacks" against Muslims, while the police and government authorities often respond inadequately.

In China, the German government identifies a "significant tightening of the legal framework of state control at the expense of freedom of religion and belief." According to the report, this particularly affects Uyghurs, Tibetans and churches that lack official state approval and are subject to harsh measures by the authorities. The law on the "Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress," which came into force on July 1, 2026, subordinates religion to "the formation of national identity" and patriotic education.

One of the countries where the situation has deteriorated most dramatically is Nicaragua, which has severely restricted freedom of religion and belief since 2018. The repression has primarily targeted the Catholic Church. According to the report, "intimidation, persecution, imprisonment, and expulsion" have forced around 130 priests and nuns to leave the country.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The reports reserves some of its sharpest criticism for Kirill, the patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church. Under his leadership, the church has strongly supported Russia's war against Ukraine and portrayed it as a "holy war." According to the report, "weapons are blessed, Russian soldiers are absolved of their sins, and donations are collected for the war." It is perhaps the clearest example in the report of how religion can be used to justify oppression and violence.

The report explicitly addresses the threat posed by "transnational repression" (TNR), which it describes as a "growing global problem" that also affects Germany. The term refers to the persecution or intimidation of individuals by their country of origin beyond its own borders.

Ultimately, it argues, this amounts to a "continuation of domestic repression." Such "cross-border repression" has become considerably easier through the growing availability of digital means of repression, including smear campaigns on social media and spyware.

These forms of pressure range from physical attacks on individuals to digital assaults such as online intimidation and defamation. In some cases, repression is also carried out by threatening family members who remain in the country of origin. Russia and Iran, for example, are identified as the "main perpetrators of transnational repression" in Germany.

China is a particularly prominent example of religious and ideological tensions. Repression by Beijing in Germany primarily targets members of groups that the country's Communist Party classifies as "hostile to the system." These include Uyghurs, Tibetans, and members of the Falun Gong movement. According to the report, they are "also subject to surveillance and repressive measures in Germany," while relatives living in China are pressured.

Thomas Rachel hopes the newly published report will be "discussed in as many Bundestag committees as possible" and that members of parliament will "engage with the issue accordingly." Previous government reports on the subject have been debated in the Bundestag plenary at least once and, in some cases, twice.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The issue's place within the German government has also changed during the current legislative term. Commissioner Thomas Rachel is now based at the Foreign Ministry, while both of his predecessors since 2018 were attached to the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development. Today, Rachel says, the importance of religion is being "taken into account" in German foreign policy. He also points to his involvement in the Foreign Ministry's diplomatic training programs.

In doing so, the government led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) reversed a structural decision made by the previous center-left coalition, which was led from 2021 to 2025 by Chancellor Olaf Scholz of the Social Democratic Party (SPD). The Scholz government had reduced the issue's prominence by assigning it to the "Religion and Foreign Policy" division. Religion and foreign policy have now regained a more prominent place within government.

One example is the current foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, who has already visited the Vatican more often than his two predecessors combined. In addition, alongside Rachel, the ministry has for some time maintained a dedicated unit headed by an ambassador that deals with, among other things, "fundamental issues relating to religion and foreign policy."

#461. Jensen Huang Is Back as Nvidia CEO

Jensen Huang is stepping back into his role as chief executive of Nvidia effective immediately.

The stunning reversal comes 11 days after Huang resigned as CEO from the company he cofounded 33 years ago and after multiple declarations from the board of directors that it had no intention of reinstating him. On Monday, they took a conciliatory tone.

“The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners, and customers,” said recently appointed board chair Harvey Jones in a press release announcing the decision.

In that announcement the board said it was “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia” and that it had “received input from senior levels of the United States government” on the way to its decision. On Monday morning, President Donald Trump posted that the Nvidia board “has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO.”

“I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution,” said Huang in a statement. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”

Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO on November 12, and longtime chief financial officer Colette Kress was installed as his interim replacement. Five days later, Huang publicly announced that he was open to resuming his role as chief executive, noting the “outpouring of calls” from “employees, investors, business partners, and customers” advocating for his return.

“If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote.

The day Huang resigned, many Nvidia employees spoke up in his support. As reported by WIRED, employees left more than 1,600 comments on an internal “suggestion box” post in which they urged the company’s board to reinstall him as CEO.

In the days following, a public petition calling for Huang’s reinstatement began circulating. At the time of writing, it has amassed more than 200,000 online signatures, the majority of whom self-identified as Nvidia shareholders. Tech elites like Elon Musk and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan have claimed that they were going to sign the petition or had signed it.

Huang’s reinstatement marks a total reversal from the public stance of Nvidia’s board of directors, which said during the company’s November 17 earnings call that it “does not intend” to reinstate him as CEO. WIRED has further reported that the board was alarmed by what one source described as Huang’s “lying” over the last year or so.

President Donald Trump, who developed a close working relationship with Huang during his second administration, had indicated openness to Huang returning as CEO. Trump told reporters on November 16 that he “would not mind” if Huang returned as chief executive, adding that he believed he had “learned a big lesson.”

Huang’s resignation followed days of scrutiny over several extramarital romantic relationships: one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who has no known relation to Jensen, one with an Nvidia employee who directly reported to Huang, and one with a different Nvidia employee.

Huang’s relationship with Alice became the subject of particularly intense focus on November 6, when The New York Times and Financial Times reported that US intelligence officials suspected that Alice may be an asset of the Chinese Ministry of State Security, both citing an intelligence briefing that circulated among top Trump administration officials last year. In the days since, some reports and Trump administration officials have questioned the accuracy of that intelligence. The Chinese government has consistently rejected claims that Alice was one of its spies.

Alice was the chief executive of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI company that’s been accused of helping Chinese tech companies use Nvidia’s most advanced chips at overseas locations, effectively sidestepping US export restrictions. Alice has also reportedly worked as a television reporter, at HSBC’s Hong Kong-based private banking arm, and at an investment bank backed by the Chinese state.

Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, purportedly with the mission of bringing realistic 3D graphics to personal computers. For many years, the company was primarily known within the gaming community. It didn’t become a household name until the recent AI boom, when its graphics processing units (GPUs) became a crucial piece of infrastructure for powering advanced AI models.

Nvidia controlled about 90 percent of the global GPU market as of September 2026. The year prior, it became the first company to be valued at more than $4 trillion, though its stock price has been in precipitous decline since Huang’s resignation.
